newsitem.title: UK: Britain's June rainfall highest since 1860.
newsitem.headline: Britain's June rainfall highest since 1860.

text.p: Britain has had the wettest June since 1860, after the worst dry spell in 200 years earlier this year, according to the U.K. Meteorological Office.
But even though farmers are beginning to worry they have had too much rain recently, it has still not been enough to replenish low ground water stocks.
A total of 133.7 millimetres of rain fell in June compared with 150 millimetres in 1860 and the June average of 65 millimetres, a spokesman for the Meteorological Office said.
The year started with the worst dry spell for 200 years which left ground water reserves severely depleted.

June's rain will not make any great difference to reserves, a spokeswoman for the Environment Agency said. But it was welcome because it means a reduction in demand as farmers need less irrigation and householders do not need to water their gardens, she said.

But in the particularly badly affected East Anglia region, where supplies come from groundwater, it would make no difference. "Ground water resources don't improve no matter how much it rains (at this time of year)," she said.
After the month of April, increased evaporation, increased plant growth and increased consumption meant that heavy rain was little help, she explained.
The rain was needed during the winter months, she said.
"I don't think the water table has come up very much," an East Anglian farming source agreed. But there were signs that farmers' own reservoirs were being replenished by run-off from the fields.

The wet weather was helping sugar beet and potatoes to develop, but there were worries over the barley crop. "Some of the barley is a bit flat," she said. There were concerns over quality and the possibility of a difficult harvest because of the wet weather.
Lack of sunshine was holding back some cereals crops, she said.
But wheat still looked good. "It all depends what happens in the next two or three weeks," she said.

Britain's rain is not a result of the developing El Nino phenomenon, which raises sea temperatures off South America and can affect the weather all around the world, a Meteorological Office spokesman said. El Nino is linked with drought in southern Africa and Australia and wet weather in California --Christopher Lyddon, London newsroom +44 171 542 7928
